extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, media researchers, and policymakers interested in media ethics and misinformation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating undercover/hidden‑camera investigative videos and the organizations that produce them (accuracy, legality, sourcing, editing, transparency, and ethical impact). Applicable to journalists, fact‑checkers, and media watchdogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal compliance / criminality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the filmmakers or operatives committed crimes while producing the videos (e.g., fraud, entering federal property under false pretenses, wiretapping, or other statutory violations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page cites investigations and prosecutions as evidence: Title 42 (prohibiting procuring ballots fraudulently), arrests for entering federal property under false pretenses (Senator Landrieu office), a jury finding Project Veritas violated wiretapping laws and misrepresented itself to Democracy Partners, reduced charges, convictions, settlements, and civil suits (defamation). Use official investigatory findings and court outcomes to assess legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and truthful representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether videos accurately represent what targets said or did, or whether excerpts/montage create false impressions (e.g., falsely implying job roles or seniority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CNN videos that 'falsely implied' a medical producer had a senior decision-making role; Pfizer video allegations denied by Pfizer and judged implausible by scientists. Evaluate full context, subject statements, and third‑party fact checks to judge accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context completeness / deceptive editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether material omits context or is edited in a way that changes the meaning of spoken words or events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly notes that 'the videos' accuracy was questioned for possibly omitting context' and that 'unedited raw footage has not been made available.' Examples: CNN/Van Jones/Jimmy Carr clips allegedly taken out of context; Minnesota Snapchat clips allegedly edited/combined. When raw footage is unavailable or key framing is omitted, treat claims with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration and evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether allegations in the videos are corroborated by independent evidence or sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Amy Robach/ABC story 'lacked sufficient corroboration'; Snopes, USA Today, and The New York Times found Project Veritas material 'lack[ed] evidence' or 'no verifiable evidence.' Good practice: require independent documentation, records, or multiple credible witnesses before accepting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the credibility, credentials, and reliability of individuals featured in recordings (e.g., whether they are who they claim to be or have relevant authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Omar Jamal described as 'uncredentialed' and disputed claims about his affiliations; postal worker Richard Hopkins later recanted. Verify identity, institutional affiliation, and prior reliability; be wary of self‑described titles that cannot be confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: release of raw/unedited footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the outlet releases raw, unedited recordings to allow independent verification of editing and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snopes requested raw footage but Project Veritas refused; lack of raw footage prevented independent verification of edits and translations. Releasing full recordings/transcripts improves credibility; refusal is a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with recording/wiretapping laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the method of obtaining recordings violated wiretapping, eavesdropping, or other recording laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes a jury found Project Veritas 'violated wiretapping laws and misrepresented itself' and later appeals. Evaluate relevant jurisdictional recording statutes and any court findings about illegal recording or misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement vs. documentation (entrapment/creation of wrongdoing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether operatives merely documented wrongdoing or actively induced, suggested, or proposed illegal acts to targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Patrick Moran was allegedly proposed a plan by someone posing as supporter; investigations sometimes concluded no charges. Distinguish between subjects volunteering wrongdoing and operatives soliciting or engineering illegal behavior; inducement undermines credibility and may be illegal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of translation and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether translations of non‑English material are accurate and verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Minnesota videos, Snopes 'could not verify the accuracy of the Somali to English translations' used by Project Veritas. When translations are central to allegations, independent language verification is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of evidence for criminal or regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the available facts support referral, prosecution, or administrative penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: special prosecutors concluded there was 'no applicable criminal offense' and 'insufficient evidence' in the Battleground Texas case; New Hampshire AG dropped its investigation. Use prosecutorial reports and inspector general findings to judge sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic ethics and good‑faith practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether methods and motives align with accepted journalistic norms (truthfulness, fairness, minimizing harm) or reflect 'bad faith' deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ACLU noted Project Veritas' 'disgraceful deceptions' even while cautioning about government overreach; critics described operations as 'operat[ing] in bad faith.' Evaluate intent, proportionality, and adherence to newsroom ethical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on subjects and downstream harms
rubrics_metrics.description: The real-world consequences of publishing the material: firings, resignations, arrests, legal actions, reputational damage, or public disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: employees resigned or were fired (PBS lawyer, Americans United for Change contractor), arrests resulted from alleged plots shown in videos, defamation suits filed. Consider harm vs. public interest when judging whether publication was responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and timing with political actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the release of material appears coordinated with political campaigns or actors, affecting independence and motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers flagged 'questions of coordination' when Project Veritas' Minnesota material was shared almost simultaneously by Trump campaign figures. Check timestamps, prior access, and sharing networks to assess coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to corrections and recantations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the outlet corrects course, retracts claims, or stops promoting material once key elements are discredited or sources recant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after the Erie postal worker recanted and official reports found no evidence, Project Veritas 'continued to promote the postal worker's claims.' Responsible publishers update or retract when evidence undermines claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unidentified or anonymous sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on unidentified individuals whose statements cannot be independently validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times noted Project Veritas used 'only unidentified sources' in some stories. Heavy reliance on anonymous sources without corroboration reduces reliability; document attempts to verify or explain anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision‑making and thresholds for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms' internal standards about whether material meets thresholds for publication (e.g., corroboration, sourcing) and when to withhold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABC said the Amy Robach story 'lacked sufficient corroboration at that time' and thus was not broadcast. Editorial standards should be explicit about corroboration, legal risk, and verification before publishing undercover material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and framing accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether titles, headlines, and video labels accurately summarize what the content shows or misleadingly imply connections that evidence does not support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: YouTube titles implying Ilhan Omar 'connected' harvesters when clips did not show that link; misleading titles can amplify false impressions even if clips are ambiguous. Match headlines to verifiable content.
